title: Why do we say 'bury the hatchet'?

entries.note: Not from Royal Navy boys born between a ship's cannons, as Admiral William Henry Smyth claimed; probably a minced euphemism for a ruder phrase, chosen because gun rhymes with son.
Compares someone to a cannon come unlashed on a warship in rough seas; spread by [[see:Victor Hugo]]'s 1874 novel [[see:Ninety-Three]], with its chapter about a runaway cannon.
Originally the literal image of a murderer with a just-fired weapon, first in [[see:Arthur Conan Doyle]]'s The Adventure of the Gloria Scott; popularised by talk of Nixon during [[see:Watergate]].
From Scottish criminal law, where [[from:taken red hand]] appears in the 1470s for homicide and later poaching; [[see:Walter Scott]] spread the shortened red-handed in Ivanhoe (1819).
A medieval Latin legal phrase that pairs with [[see:smoking gun]] and [[see:caught red-handed]], though it suggests arson rather than weapons.
From archery, not violins: a spare bowstring in case the first snaps, so it originally meant backup options rather than extra skills; Henry VIII's state papers (1524) recommend two strings.
From customs of wearing feathers as marks of achievement; a 1599 account says Hungarians wore one feather for each Turk they had killed.

entries.term: too many irons in the fire
entries.note: From blacksmithing: with too many irons heating at once, one can burn until it becomes unworkable.

entries.term: strike while the iron is hot
entries.note: From blacksmithing, where you must hammer iron into shape while it is hot; the dictionary's earliest citation is Geoffrey Chaucer, around 1405.
Middle English [[from:loupe]] was a narrow slit in a fortification for archers or musketeers; the fortification sense appears in 1591, and gaps in laws by the 1660s.
From a diplomatic custom among North American Indigenous nations, especially the [[see:Iroquois Confederacy]], of burying war axes to make peace, though the record is largely oral.
From axe heads flying off their handles, perhaps unreliable axes in some war; the hosts can't see how it came to mean losing your temper.
A military inspection, as in pass muster, from the Latin verb to show via Old French [[from:monstrer]]; gathering people is named after the muster, not the other way round.
German for a sample, such as a carpet sample; in most European languages this cognate of English [[same-root:muster]] means a sample, example or template.
French for to show, from the same Latin verb that gave English [[same-root:muster]].
A TikTok commenter asked why it contains a [[unrelated:demon]]; it doesn't, but it does contain [[same-root:monster]], from the old French word meaning to show.
Originally something you point at in alarm, from the same old French word meaning to show that gave [[same-root:muster]].
Not a corruption involving [[unrelated:muster]] but about harvesting the tall, tricky mustard plant; an 1884 citation has cut mustard, and the article came later.
Coined by [[see:John Gay]] as the first simile in his 1732 poem A New Song of New Similes, which also gave [[see:cool as a cucumber]].
Discussed in an earlier episode; coined by [[see:John Gay]] in the same 1732 poem as [[see:mustard strong]].
Named for its intense flavour, at least in its intensifying [[from:-ard]] ending, as the hosts have discussed before.
An intensifying ending, cited for [[see:mustard]]; the hosts joke that it comes up so often it needs its own bell.
An idiom the hosts jokingly coin, meaning to bring up that one idiom or the [[see:-ard]] ending yet again.
Firing off a load of things at once, offered as Jess keeps firing off gun idioms.
From a 1936 speech by [[see:Joseph Goebbels]] framing a trade-off between military spending and civilian goods; now shorthand for balancing defence and domestic budgets.
A macroeconomic model of a nation's investment in defence versus civilian goods, inspired by [[from:guns and butter]].
Originally reward plus punishment, as in [[see:Winston Churchill]]'s 1938 letter on Austria; the image of a carrot dangled from a stick comes from later cartoons.
First found in Francis Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue, spelt like [[see:monkey]] but pronounced dunkey; probably a pet form of [[from?:Duncan]], like [[see:jackass]] and [[see:neddy]].
Francis Grose spelt [[see:donkey]] to match monkey, though donkey was then pronounced dunkey.
Jack is a name, which shows how donkeys get people's names and supports the [[see:Duncan]] theory of [[see:donkey]].
Another name used for donkeys, cited with [[see:jackass]] and [[see:neddy]] as support for the [[see:Duncan]] theory of [[see:donkey]].
Another name-based word for donkeys, cited with [[see:jackass]] as support for the [[see:Duncan]] theory of [[see:donkey]].
A name meaning dark, which Jess says would suit a donkey's dun fur and supports the theory that it gave [[gave?:donkey]].
The German word for dark, which Rob compares with [[see:Duncan]], a name said to mean dark.
From armed guards beside stagecoach drivers in the 19th-century American West, exaggerated by 1880s Western fiction; the shotgun seat then became the front passenger seat of any car.
Under intense pressure; popularised by poker, where the player who acts first in each betting round, with no information, sits under the gun.
A phrase similar to [[see:under the gun]], meaning under pressure or at risk of punishment.
The next level of intensity after [[see:under the gun]]: actively dodging problems as they come your way.
Comes from [[from:Damocles]], as the hosts note in passing after [[see:under fire]].
An early 19th-century way to refer to a family secret, first recorded in [[see:William Makepeace Thackeray]]'s writing, and probably a callback to [[see:Bluebeard]].
[[see:Charles Perrault]]'s 1697 tale of a man who kills his wives and hides their corpses; dictionaries have listed bluebeard as a wife-murderer since the 1700s.
Listed in some sources as the crime of killing, or seducing and abandoning, a series of women, after [[from:Bluebeard]].
Recorded in 1616 for someone pleading for Satan's kingdom; the Catholic Church's term for whoever argued against a canonisation or miracle probably gave the modern sense.
One of the many idioms involving the [[see:devil]] that the hosts call relatively self-explanatory.

entries.term: devil finds work for idle hands
entries.note: One of the many idioms involving the [[see:devil]] that the hosts call relatively self-explanatory.
Imagines the devil as a hypothetical being who might care about consequences, implying that no one worth worrying about cares at all.
Doesn't have to mean the Devil, since it can be any demon or pixie-like being; it is often used as an emphatic expletive, which is behind many idioms.

entries.term: between the devil and the deep blue sea
entries.note: A dilemma between two dangerous options, like [[see:Scylla and Charybdis]] or [[equivalent:a precipice ahead and wolves behind]]; the devil may stand for death or anything very bad.

entries.term: a precipice ahead and wolves behind
entries.note: One of the older proverbs about two dangers, similar to the English [[equivalent:between the devil and the deep blue sea]].
A hidden reference to the [[see:devil]], which the hosts say they have discussed a lot before.
An example of using the [[see:devil]] as an emphatic expletive.
An example of using the [[see:devil]] as an emphatic expletive.
An example of using the [[see:devil]] as an emphatic expletive.

entries.term: wear your heart on your sleeve
entries.note: First clearly recorded in [[see:Othello]]; Merriam-Webster suggests it alludes to medieval knights wearing a lady's token on their armoured sleeve when jousting.
One of many idioms that move the heart around the body, since the heart was seen as the seat of life, mind, will and courage.
Echoes the physical feeling of fear, when you can feel your heartbeat rising in your chest.
Used when fear rises and the heart climbs into your mouth, echoing what fear feels like physically.
Another historical placement of the heart, which was treated as the seat of life, mind and will.
Where the heart is supposed to be, the hosts joke, among all the idioms that move it around the body.
Used when your courage fails, echoing the stomach-dropping feeling of fear.
Describes the feeling of your whole body sinking, another idiom that moves the heart around.
Means heart-shaped; Rob uses it to lead into [[see:pyriform]] and [[see:go pear-shaped]].
RAF slang, probably from a botched loop-the-loop ending in a pear shape, or perhaps a stall; the OED's earliest citation is surprisingly recent, from 1983.
Means pear-shaped; Rob suggests saying it's all gone a bit pyriform as a more sophisticated [[see:go pear-shaped]].
From [[from:snakes and ladders]], according to the OED; first recorded in 1952 in the Economic Journal, which compared a complicated argument to the game.
From sports where a [[from:scratch]] line marked the start; it means starting without any head start or handicap, not quite the same as [[see:back to square one]].
The starting line in running races and boxing matches, literally a line etched into the floor; in golf it means no handicap, and cricket's [[see:crease]] was once called the scratch.
Cricket's crease was in the past known as the [[see:scratch]].
From boxing, where fighters came up to a line drawn on the ground, ready to fight; [[see:Charles Dickens]] wrote come up to the scratch in an 1843 letter.
